items.title: Tranched yield, power perps, tokenized stocks and new launchpads led what shipped this week.
items.summary:
Tranched yield, power perps, tokenized stocks and new launchpads led what shipped this week.

Here are 8 crypto apps worth testing this week 🧠👇

1. @mezzanine_fi: Mezzanine splits one DeFi strategy into a junior and a senior vault, so you pick your risk. Its first vault, the @HastraFi Optimizer, loops yield from auto loans and US home equity loans across Morpho and Kamino. It hit $4.81M TVL in its first 24h, with senior at ~18% and junior at ~38% APY (variable).

Junior absorbs losses first, and the yield comes from private credit, so borrower risk is real.

2. @tradeparagon: Paragon lists 24/7 perps on @HyperliquidX for stocks, Treasury yields and pre-IPO names like Anthropic. This week it unveiled Power Perps, starting with HYPE²: if HYPE doubles, the index quadruples, with no strikes and no expiry.

Longs usually pay funding for that convexity, so HYPE can rise and you can still lose. Check that HYPE² is tradeable in the app before sizing in.

3. @eqxlabs: EQX issues tokenized spot US stocks and ETFs on Hyperliquid, from SPY and QQQ to NVDA and SpaceX, each backed 1:1 by shares held at StoneX, Clear Street and Alpaca. It adds no issuer fees on top of Hyperliquid's trading fee, and with equity perp funding spiking, you can hold the spot token and short the perp to collect it.

4. @miranetwork: Sterling is an OpenAI-compatible inference API that only routes your request to providers Mira has tested, so the Claude, GPT or Gemini you pay for is the model that actually answers. Top up in USDC or $MIRA and pay as you go. The launch post passed 200k views.

5. @priors_trade: Credit lines for AI agents on Robinhood Chain. Agents borrow USDG, pay other agents for work straight from the line, and every repayment lands on a public record backers can read before extending more. 98 new agents joined last week, and 177 repaid a loan in a single 24h stretch.

Backers carry the default risk, so only back what you can afford to lose.

6. @saplingdotcash: Sapling is the first Zcash-native launchpad and trading terminal for Solana coins. You launch and trade straight from your Zcash wallet, and holders get paid in ZEC from trading fees. In its first 41 days it did $45.75M in volume across 531K+ trades, with 10,529 holders and $643.6K in protocol revenue, 90% of which went back to the community.

Most of what launches here is memecoins, and only about 6% of coins graduate, so size small.

7. @floatdotxyz: Float is a new Solana launchpad, powered by @Raydium, for coins paired with stock tokens like NVIDIA, Tesla or McDonald's, or with plain SOL or USDC. It passed $1M in fees within weeks of launch, airdropped $127.5K USDC to its top 100 traders, and has burned about 10% of the $FLOAT supply through buybacks.

It's memecoin territory, and the team is still changing the launch rules every few days, so keep size small.

8. @longdotxyz: LONG is a Robinhood Chain launchpad for coins paired with stock tokens. Since Nov 6, you can launch new stock-token pairs straight from the @RobinhoodCrypto wallet app, with gas covered. Its AI Nexus basket (long AI names, short QQQ) now lets holders vote on what's in it every 7 days and earn a share of its trading fees.

DYOR/NFA.

Anything we should test this week?

## Over time, AI is going to turn our brains to mush. People won't be able to remember phone numbers, basic grammar or directions to places they've visited once or twice without consulting AI overlords.

Portrait of Blake Fontenay

There's an old episode of "The Simpsons" where Homer, the TV show's booze-addled antihero, offers a hilarious toast: "To alcohol! The cause of – and solution to – all of life's problems." [...] People – some of us, at least – are worried about AI eventually overthrowing human civilization. Even more immediately, there's widespread concern about the proliferation of data centers needed to support AI operations.

Yet at the same time we're collectively wringing our hands about those issues, we are meekly surrendering more and more control to machines over our everyday lives.

items.title: Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,
items.summary:
Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,000.

And Apple plans to cut it again.

Last month, some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported. Some engineering teams could be cut to $100 a day next. Many groups outside engineering already sit at $100, and Apple has considered going as low as $25 for some of them.

In March, Jensen said on the All-In podcast that he'd be deeply alarmed if a $500,000 engineer used less than $250,000 of AI tokens in a year. He also said Dario Amodei's forecast of hundreds of billions in AI revenue was too conservative.

So Jensen's rule is simple: AI spending should run about half of what an engineer gets paid.

By my math, at about 250 workdays a year, $200 a day comes to roughly $50,000. The planned $100 cap comes to roughly $25,000.

By Jensen's rule, a $100 daily cap only makes sense for an engineer paid about $50,000 a year.

And Apple still wants its people using MORE AI. It's steering teams toward cheaper models and AI that runs on the device, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said Apple's internal work runs heavily on Anthropic's models.

I think Apple just showed where the real limit on the AI boom sits now: The finance department.

And that's just ONE company:

- Accenture capped Claude at $29 a month per employee on October 1, after some staff had been spending up to $1,000 a month, 404 Media reported.
- Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in about 4 months, then capped AI coding tools at $1,500 a month per tool.
- Microsoft has cut allowances too, and its AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Bloomberg that Anthropic is extremely expensive and that Microsoft wants to eventually get rid of that cost.
- Meta had internal leaderboards ranking staff by how many tokens they used, and now it has introduced token budgets.

The usage is clearly there. Uber's engineers used the tools so much they spent a full year's budget in 4 months.

So the people saying stop are the ones paying the bill.

That's a huge problem for the AI labs, for one reason: Their spending is already locked in. 

Anthropic has committed to $895 billion, mostly for computing power. OpenAI has signed more than $1.4 trillion of compute deals. And paying for all of it depends on companies spending more on AI per worker every year.

Apple, Accenture, Uber and Microsoft all pay for Anthropic's models, and Anthropic could start its IPO roadshow as early as next week. Its own filing shows revenue grew about 47% from the second quarter to the third, down from about 144% the quarter before, and price cuts took about $600 million out of revenue.

Plenty of people will say this is just housekeeping, and they have numbers:

Bloomberg says few Apple engineers ever used the full $300, so the savings may be small. Cheaper models can do the same work for less. Apple's R&D still rose 32% to $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026, partly because of AI. And more companies start using AI every month, so total spending can keep growing even with a cap on each worker.

But Jensen's pitch depends on spending per worker going UP. Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Accenture are all writing rules that push it down.

So the first question for Anthropic's roadshow should be simple: How much are its biggest customers spending per employee compared with a year ago, and how many of them have put caps in place?

Who's right about what an engineer's AI is worth, Jensen Huang or Apple's finance team?

items.title: Your AI coding agent writes a plan.
items.summary:
Your AI coding agent writes a plan.

Then it reviews its plan.

It's the same session, with the same context and the same blind spots.

Google engineers created a fix for this, and it's now open source.
It's called the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM). It uses two types of sessions:
→ Elephant = a long session that remembers everything. It contains the entire design. No code is written here.
→ Goldfish = new sessions with zero memory. They just read the spec and live code, without any chat history to bias them.

How it works, in 3 phases:

Phase 1 · Brainstorm (egm-brainstorm)
→ The agent interviews you about the feature
→ "No code" rule: You first debate the trade-offs and challenge the assumptions

Phase 2 · Draft (egm-draft)
→ Writes a Markdown design doc
→ Problem, technical plan, considered alternatives, and exact files to change

Phase 3 · Review (egm-review)
→ Comprehension check: A fresh Goldfish must explain the plan back to you. If they can't, the doc isn't clear.
→ Hostile review: Several Goldfish attack the doc for edge cases, hidden dependencies, and logic gaps. Their notes go back to the Elephant.
→ Readiness check: A final Goldfish check checks whether the file path, data structure, and function signature are all there.

Then the agent writes the code.

Setup:

Cloud Code
Cloud Plugin Marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
Cloud Plugin install egm@egm

Codex
Codex Plugin Marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
Codex Plugin add egm@egm

Antigravity
agy Plugin install + repo link (in reply)

Another agent: Ask them to install the plugin from the repo link.

Things to know:
→ Free, Apache 2.0 license
→ Google says thousands of its engineers use it daily to ship production code
→ The README states that it is not an officially supported Google product
→ It is designed for features that require design decisions. For a small bug fix, just prompt normally.

I believe:
This morning's paper found that the best coding agent met 69.9% of requirements but only completed 26.4% of tasks completely.

Agents often fail to write down details that no one has written down.

In EGM, you have to write down the details before the agent even touches a single file.

REPOO 👇

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.

# Australia to launch AI safety regulator after OpenAI’s breach of a government portal

By 

ROD McGUIRK

The Associated Press

MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday. [...] OpenAI apologized in September for the breach and its slow response.

“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We also should have handled our response better.”

## Inquiry recommends possible criminal law changes

A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law. [...] Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the U.S. company took too long to inform the government in September that a rogue agent had infiltrated government websites three months earlier, which was the first occurrence of such a breach with the technology.

Information taken without authorization from the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 has since been made public. It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.
